sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Large language model (LLM) agents now work over horizons far longer than single context window (Luo et al., 2025b; Huang et al., 2026b). personal agent accumulates months of conversation with its user, and task agent meets similar problems across many episodes. Memory lets such agents carry information across sessions (Wang et al., 2025a), so that they can personalize their responses (Zhang et al., 2026e), stay consistent with what they were told (Packer et al., 2023; Chhikara et al., 2025), and reuse what worked before (Wang et al., 2025e; Xia et al., 2026a). Benchmarks now measure this ability on long conversations (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025), long documents (Hu et al., 2026), multi-session agentic tasks (He et al., 2026), and lifelong personalization (Zhang et al., 2026d). Benchmarks score memory by its answers, but team that deploys one asks more of it. memory that agents can rely on in practice has to meet three requirements at once. It has to be accurate about the particulars of past experience, such as name, date, count, or the distinction between two events, and about the connections between them. It has to be practical, which means deployable with the models team already uses, nothing to train, answers that can be traced to stored records, and consolidation that cannot destroy what was stored. It also has to be efficient, with answer latency and token cost per question that stay bounded as the history grows. Each family of existing systems gives up at least one of the three. Systems that consolidate records into extracted facts or abstractions (Chhikara et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026) are compact but give up accuracy: the details they discard are gone for good, and consolidation can make memory faulty even when it is distilled from useful experience (Zhang et al., 2026a). Systems that keep every record and retrieve from them directly lose nothing but give up efficiency, since retrieval must search an ever larger and noisier history (Huang et al., 2026b). Graph memories organize the same content around entities and their relations (Rasmussen et al., 2025; Edge et al., 2024), but binary triples split an n-ary fact into fragments and lose the connections among its participants (Luo et al., 2025a). Hypergraph memories (Yue et al., 2026) group episodes under topics and facts under episodes, but their hyperedges record which unit belongs where rather than the participants of fact, and retrieval descends from topic summaries written at storage time, so detail is reachable only after its topic has been retrieved. File-system memories, such as the auto memory of Claude Code (Anthropic, 2026), route retrieval through summaries in the same way: they keep notes in plain files behind size-capped index that is loaded into every session, and the agent opens file on the strength of its one-line summary. detail that no summary mentions is reachable only by string search, which neither resolves an entity across files nor follows its relations, and index entries past the cap are not loaded at the start of session. Both families prune top down to bound their cost, and both pay for the pruning with recall on details their summaries do not reflect. Parametric memories store experience in model weights or latent states (Wang et al., 2024b, 2025b,c; Behrouz et al., 2025) and give up practicality, since they require training and rule out closed models. The requirements also weigh differently for the two uses of memory. Recent studies separate user-centric memory, which personalizes an agent to its user, from agent-centric memory, which accumulates the agents own experience, and they find that the two face reversed challenges (Huang et al., 2026b,c). user-centric memory has to record users history broadly and connect its pieces, because later question may depend on any detail of that history (Zhang et al., 2026d; Ma et al., 2026b). An agent-centric memory has to be precise and refined instead. It distills trajectories into strategies and skills (Zhao et al., 2024; Ouyang et al., 2026; Xia et al., 2026b), and retrieving too much can pull the agents attention away from the context that matters for its next action (Huang et al., 2026c). practical system has to serve both uses from one store. Figures 2 and 3 trace one example of each setting through MIRIX-2.0. In this work, we present MIRIX-2.0, multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It keeps the multi-agent design of MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) and rethinks how memory is stored, indexed, retrieved, and consolidated so that specific layer meets each requirement (Figure 1). Six memory agents under Meta Memory Manager write complete records to typed evidence plane in vector database, the system of record, so details survive consolidation and every graph fact the answer receives cites the rows it came from. The graph is only an index. The database write commits first, failed graph write never rolls back stored memory, and failed graph read falls back to direct evidence retrieval. provenance hypergraph indexes the entities, events, relations, roles, and times in episodic and semantic records Figure 2 User-centric memory. Sessions are stored as episodic and semantic records, and later question retrieves graph facts with their source rows to give personalized answer. as n-ary frames that cite the rows they were extracted from and carry dates, prices, and counts as literals, and undated events with similar wording keep distinct identities. At query time, deterministic planner sets explicit budgets, retrieval enters the hypergraph at the anchors that match the question, and the answer receives graph facts together with the records they cite (Section 2.4). The evidence question inspects is therefore bounded by construction and does not grow with the length of the history. Like sleep-time and offline consolidation methods (Lin et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), AutoDream consolidates memory outside the write path, and it treats the two kinds of memory in opposite ways. For semantic memory, it consolidates identities and never rewrites evidence. It pairs each anchor introduced by new semantic rows with its nearest anchors of the same identity-stable type, such as person or place, and asks language model whether pair denotes one entity. confirmed merge unites the citations of the two anchors and rewires the frames that mention them, while event anchors, fact frames, and stored records stay unchanged, so merge can never destroy stored memory. Its cost depends on the newly written semantic frontier rather than on the total size of memory, verification runs under explicit pair caps, and negative decisions are cached so that later cycles do not pay for the same pair again. For procedural memory, AutoDream refines instead. It judges each finished task session from quotes in its transcript, distills lessons worth reusing and mistakes worth avoiding, and lets curator (Zhang et al., 2026c) create or edit skills whose edits can cite the experiences behind them. We evaluate MIRIX-2.0 on conversational memory, long-document question answering, personalized generation, and procedural memory for interactive agents. MIRIX-2.0 has the highest accuracy of all compared memory systems on both conversational benchmarks, 91.4% on LoCoMo in our runs and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, 14.3 points above the strongest baseline. On LoCoMo, the hypergraph raises accuracy over flat memory from 85.7% to 88.4%, with the largest gain on multi-hop questions, and AutoDream raises every question type and lifts the overall score to 91.4%. On LongMemEval-S, the hypergraph alone adds 11.2 points. On the single-hop and multi-hop document QA tasks of MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026), with AutoDream disabled, it answers 83.0% and 71.0% of the questions, 31.0 and 22.0 points above the strongest baseline, and on MemoryCD (Zhang et al., 2026d) it has the highest value on all four metrics for cross-domain review summarization. Used as procedural memory, MIRIX-2.0 gives the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), at 76.4% with GPT-6 Luna against 73.6% for Agent Workflow Memory (AWM) (Wang et al., 2025e) and 69.4% without memory, and on WebShop (Yao et al., 2022), at 37.4%. With GPT-5.2 it reaches 49.2% accuracy on MetaClaw-Bench (Xia et al., 2026b), against 44.0% reported for the MetaClaw skill library. 3 What makes these results usable is the cost at which they come. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem, the strongest baseline, on all five benchmarks we timed, ingests the two conversational benchmarks in less time, and uses fewer answer tokens on four of the five. As procedural memory, on WebShop it uses the fewest training and test tokens among the memory methods while reaching the highest success. The cost is paid when long documents are ingested. Building the graph makes their ingestion about four times slower than flat memory and slower than that baseline. The full system with AutoDream is not timed, and the retrieval bounds cover the evidence question inspects, not latency measured as the history grows. No model is fine-tuned, the same system runs with closed and open models, and the code is public. Our contributions are as follows. Accurate and practical. layered memory design in which six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record and provenance-preserving n-ary hypergraph serves only as their index, with occurrence identities that keep distinct events apart and fail-soft indexing that never rolls back stored memory. One memory for users and agents. To the best of our knowledge, MIRIX-2.0 is the first memory system that handles both user-centric and agent-centric memory, serving personalization and the refinement of agent skills from one store. Efficient and safe to consolidate. Graph-owned retrieval runs under explicit budgets and returns graph facts together with the records that justify them. AutoDream merges duplicate entity anchors under explicit caps without touching stored memories, which adds 3.0 points on LoCoMo, and distills task sessions into skills for procedural memory. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents MIRIX-2.0. It states the problem and the three technical requirements, introduces the typed evidence plane and the provenance hypergraph that indexes it, describes graph-owned retrieval under explicit budgets, and explains how AutoDream consolidates semantic and procedural memory outside the write path. Section 3 evaluates the accuracy of MIRIX-2.0 on conversational recall, long-document question answering, and personalized generation, its use as agent memory on ALFWorld, WebShop, and MetaClaw-Bench, and its cost in ingestion time, answer latency, and tokens. Section 4 relates MIRIX-2.0 to prior work on memory systems for LLM agents, multi-agent systems, and memory consolidation, and Section 5 concludes and discusses the limitations of this study. Section gives the details of the method, and Section gives the full results behind the figures.

sections.title: 2 Methodology
sections.content: MIRIX-2.0 is designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient. It has to run with the models team already uses and leave stored records intact, it has to keep name, date, count, or the distinction between two events recoverable after writing and after consolidation, and it has to answer from bounded evidence set however long the history grows. This section describes the layered design that delivers the three. MIRIX-2.0 separates storage from indexing (Figure 1). typed evidence plane stores complete memories and is the system of record (Section 2.2). provenance hypergraph indexes the entities, events, relations, roles, and times in those memories, and every fact in it cites the records it came from (Section 2.3). Three paths operate on the two layers, and Algorithm 1 states each of them in pseudocode. The write path stores memory and then indexes it. The read path plans query, traverses the graph, and dereferences only the records it selects (Section 2.4). AutoDream, the third path, runs outside the other two (Section 2.5). On semantic memory it merges duplicate anchors in the hypergraph and returns the evidence store unchanged, so semantic consolidation changes how evidence is connected, never what evidence exists. On procedural memory, AutoDream instead distills task sessions into skills that cite the experiences behind them. Section A.6 collects the properties that hold regardless of how the language models behave. 4 Figure 3 Agent-centric memory. AutoDream turns failed purchase into experiences and revised routine, which later task follows to meet every constraint.

sections.title: 3 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate MIRIX-2.0 for the three properties it is designed for. Accuracy is measured for user memory on conversational recall, document QA, and personalized generation (Section 3.2), which mainly exercise semantic memory together with the episodic records that ground it, and for agent memory on held-out interactive tasks and on MetaClaw-Bench, whose tasks span 30 days (Section 3.3), which exercise procedural memory. Efficiency is measured as ingestion time, answer latency, and answer tokens for user memory, with AutoDream disabled in every timed run, and as training and test tokens for agents (Section 3.4). Practicality is built into the protocol itself. One system serves both uses, no model is fine-tuned, the agent evaluation covers closed and open backbones, and every graph configuration runs under the budgets of Section 2.4.

The available document QA results and graph efficiency measurements use M1 and are labeled accordingly; disabling AutoDream there is an experimental choice, not restriction that prevents consolidation of document memories. MemoryCD is reported under the system name, but its recorded results do not identify an M0, M1, or M2 configuration, so we do not use them to estimate the contribution of AutoDream. For agent memory, we evaluate the procedural refinement 9 path, in which AutoDream distills sessions into reusable skills whose retrieval is independent of the semantic hypergraph. The M0, M1, and M2 comparisons below therefore concern user-memory indexing and semantic consolidation, rather than procedural graph ablation. User-memory tasks and baselines. LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024) and LongMemEval-S (Wu et al., 2025) test conversational recall. SHDocQA, MHDocQA, and DetectiveQA in the MemoryAgentBench evaluation (Hu et al., 2026) extend this analysis to factual and relational evidence in documents. They are evidence-retrieval tests rather than direct personalization tasks. MemoryCD (Zhang et al., 2026d) tests whether stored user information supports personalized review summarization and generation. We compare with mem0, A-Mem, MemoryBank, Graphiti, and HyperMem on QA, and with the methods listed in the MemoryCD tables, including long-context and RAG baselines, on personalization. Models and scoring. For the user-memory evaluation, the answerer and extractor use gpt-4.1-mini with temperature 0 and seed 42, and the topic extractor uses gpt-4.1-nano. MIRIX-2.0 uses text-embedding-3small; external baselines retain their default embeddings. SHDocQA and MHDocQA use substring matching, and DetectiveQA uses letter exact matching. LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S use gpt-4o-mini judge with majority-of-3 voting. MemoryCD uses ROUGE-1, ROUGE-L, BLEU-4, and BERTScore-F1. Agent backbones and evaluation protocols are specified in Section 3.3. Differences in accuracy or success rate are reported in percentage points. Efficiency and uncertainty. We report total ingestion wall-clock time, mean time to retrieve and answer question, total answer tokens, and graph node and edge counts where available. Graph size measures index structure, not stored text length or total storage. For interactive agents, we report success, action steps, and training and test tokens, with mean and standard deviation over three runs. For LoCoMo, all comparisons below use the results in Table 1; M0, M1, and M2 are distinct system configurations, not repeated runs used to estimate variance.

sections.title: 3.2 User memory: recall, documents, and personalization

3.3 Agent memory: held-out tasks and skills
Setup and transfer to held-out tasks. We evaluate procedural memory on ALFWorld (Shridhar et al.,

methods share the actor prompt and backbone. ALFWorld uses GPT-6 Luna and GPT-5.6 Luna; WebShop
uses GPT-6 Luna. Each memory method learns from the same training tasks, 39 for ALFWorld and 40 for
WebShop. Memory is then frozen for evaluation on 134 held-out ALFWorld episodes with a 50-step cap
and 140 WebShop instructions with a 15-step cap. Results are averaged over three independent runs. The
separation between memory learning and evaluation tests reuse of acquired procedures on new tasks.
sections.content: This setting exercises the procedural branch of AutoDream (Section 2.5). Sessions supply lessons to reuse and mistakes to avoid, and curator turns those experiences into skills. Unlike semantic consolidation, which preserves the factual records and changes their index, procedural refinement changes the instructions available to the actor. The experiments evaluate the utility of that combined process; they do not separately ablate the outcome judge, experience distiller, or curator. ALFWorld: useful procedures must generalize across action sequences. Figure 6, and Table 10 in the appendix, show the highest mean overall success among the compared methods for MIRIX-2.0 with both backbones. With GPT-6 Luna it reaches 76.4%, compared with 69.4% without memory and 73.6% with AWM. With GPT-5.6 Luna it reaches 61.7%, compared with 54.2% and 58.0%, respectively. The gains over no memory are similar, at 7.0 and 7.5 points, but they are not uniform across task types (Figure 7). With GPT-6 Luna, Clean improves from 60.2% to 74.2% and Heat from 47.8% to 73.9%, while Pick, Look, and Pick Two remain below the no-memory scores. This suggests that procedures are most useful when they supply missing action structure; retrieving routine can also interfere with task the actor already handles well. 3.4 Efficiency: ingestion time, answer latency, and tokens
Graph construction moves work into ingestion. Figure 8a and Table 12 in the appendix show the
cost of organizing source records before queries arrive. Relative to M0, M1 increases ingestion time by 3.8
to 4.0 times across the three document tasks. M1 also has higher answer latency than M0 on each task, so
graph retrieval is not intrinsically cheaper than flat retrieval. Its purpose is to improve access to structured
evidence, with extraction and indexing paid in advance and additional evidence handling paid at query time.
sections.content: 13 Figure 8 Cost of user memory: (a) ingestion time and (b) answer time per question. Against HyperMem, M1 answers faster on all three document tasks (Figure 8b), at 5.45 versus 10.55 seconds on SHDocQA, 9.01 versus 10.65 on MHDocQA, and 7.24 versus 13.05 on DetectiveQA. It uses fewer answer tokens on SHDocQA and MHDocQA, but more on DetectiveQA, at 1.16M versus 0.35M. The DetectiveQA result shows that lower latency can coexist with higher token use and lower accuracy. Latency, token cost, and answer quality therefore need to be assessed separately. The available timings characterize M1, not the full M2 system. Figure 8b and Table 12 in the appendix show that M1 also has lower answer latency than HyperMem on LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S, completing the five-benchmark latency comparison. Its conversational ingestion time is lower as well, unlike the document setting. These measurements are consistent with bounded graph access keeping answer latency low, but they do not isolate the effects of candidate caps, model calls, or execution conditions. M2 adds consolidation calls and can change subsequent retrieval behavior. Its total ingestion cost, answer cost, and graph reduction must be measured directly before attaching the M1 latency claims to the full system. Node and edge counts alone likewise do not quantify evidence retention or compression. Fewer agent steps do not necessarily mean fewer tokens. Table 4 separates the cost of learning procedure from the cost of applying it, with the token accounting given in Section B.3. On WebShop, MIRIX-2.0 uses the fewest training and test tokens among the memory methods, 1.815M and 4.975M per run, while achieving the highest mean success. On ALFWorld, its 3.813M test tokens are the highest among the memory methods despite its lower mean step count. retrieved procedure can reduce interaction steps while increasing the context processed at each step. Relative to no memory, test tokens rise on both benchmarks, so procedural memory should be judged by the resulting success and reuse, rather than assumed to save tokens automatically. The reported totals do not determine how many future tasks are needed to amortize memory learning, because no varying-horizon cost study is included.

sections.title: 4 Related Work
sections.content: Memory systems for LLM agents. Memory systems for LLM agents keep past interactions outside the model and retrieve them when they become relevant (Huang et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2025a; Guo et al., 2026). Early designs rank or decay memory stream (Park et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024) or manage memory the way an operating system manages storage (Packer et al., 2023; Kang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025). Later systems extract and update salient facts (Chhikara et al., 2025), link notes into an evolving network (Xu et al., 2025), compress what they store (Fang et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a), or learn memory construction with reinforcement learning (Wang et al., 2025d; Yan et al., 2026). Graph memories organize content around entities and their relations (Bei et al., 2025; Rasmussen et al., 2025; Gutiérrez et al., 2024, 2025; Edge et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2026b), and hypergraph memories keep n-ary facts together (Luo et al., 2025a; Yue et al., 2026). Typed designs split memory by function, following cognitive accounts of episodic and semantic memory (Tulving, 1985; Pink et al., 2025). MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025) assigns six memory types to dedicated agents, and PersonaAgent (Zhang et al., 2026e) pairs episodic and semantic memory for personalization. Memory stored in model parameters or latent states (Wang et al., 2024b, 2025b,c; Behrouz et al., 2025) requires training and cannot be used with closed models. Evaluation has moved from recall over long conversations (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) to multi-session agentic tasks (Hu et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), evolving environments (Ji et al., 2026), lifelong personalization (Zhang et al., 2026d), memory audits (Ma et al., 2026b), and comparisons of memory substrates (Huang et al., 2026c). MIRIX-2.0 combines the typed and the graph directions. Complete typed records remain the system of record, provenance hypergraph serves only as their index, and every graph fact cites its source records. Multi-agent systems. Multi-agent systems divide task among LLM agents that take different roles (Guo et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b), from role-playing and conversable agents (Li et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024) to software teams and groups of experts (Hong et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024). Agents can debate (Du et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2024; Huang and Caragea, 2026), optimize their workflow (Zhuge et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), or communicate through latent representations (Yang et al., 2026). They also fail in new ways (Cemri et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026a), and one response keeps humans in the loop as collaborators (Zou et al., 2025a,b; Wu et al., 2026a). Memory in these systems mostly serves the collaboration, through shared pools, graphs of team trajectories, and sharing across users under access control (Gao and Zhang, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025a; Rezazadeh et al., 2025). MIRIX-2.0 applies the multi-agent design to memory itself. Meta Memory Manager routes each input to the agents of the six memory types, and each agent writes only the records of its own type. Self-reflection and memory consolidation. Self-reflection lets an agent improve from feedback on its own behavior without updating its weights (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2025). Experience-driven methods turn such feedback into reusable knowledge, including insights (Zhao et al., 2024), executable skills (Wang et al., 2024a), workflows (Wang et al., 2025e), reasoning strategies (Ouyang et al., 2026), and evolving playbooks and case banks (Suzgun et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Fang et al., 15 2026b; Zhou et al., 2025). Skills can co-evolve with the policy (Xia et al., 2026a,b), be verified and optimized as artifacts (Zhang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026a), or form hypergraph (Xu et al., 2026), and agents, their harnesses, and their memory architectures can improve themselves (Xia et al., 2026d,c; Liu et al., 2026b; Gao et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2025). Consolidation can also run offline, before queries arrive or while the user is inactive (Lin et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2026a; Xia et al., 2026b; Ye et al., 2026). Rewriting memory carries risks. Consolidated memories can become faulty (Zhang et al., 2026a), and defective skill can contaminate the skills distilled after it (Shang et al., 2026). AutoDream also consolidates outside the write path, but it limits what consolidation may change. On semantic memory it merges only anchors that denote the same entity and never rewrites stored records. On procedural memory it keeps judged outcome, and each experience skill edit cites, only after checking the quoted text.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented MIRIX-2.0, multi-agent memory system that keeps complete typed records, indexes them with provenance hypergraph under explicit budgets, and runs AutoDream outside the write path to merge duplicate anchors and refine skills. It leads the compared systems on four of the five QA benchmarks, two of them with AutoDream disabled, reaching 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, and it has the highest value on all four metrics for cross-domain review summarization on MemoryCD. On LoCoMo, the hypergraph and AutoDream each add accuracy over flat memory. As procedural memory, its distilled skills lead the compared memory methods in mean success on ALFWorld and WebShop, and with GPT-5.2 they reach 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% reported for the MetaClaw skill library. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers each question in less time than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks, and on WebShop its skills cost the fewest tokens among the memory methods. One store serves both uses, and the system runs with closed and open models without fine-tuning. The results suggest that memory layer can be practical, accurate, and efficient at once when complete records remain the system of record, the graph is only bounded index, and consolidation changes how evidence is connected rather than what evidence exists. Limitations. Our ablations add components in groups. They do not isolate n-ary frames, cited source rows, occurrence identities, answer-time verification, or the judge, distiller, and curator of procedural memory, so the explanations in Section 3 remain interpretations. The user-memory results come from single runs, partly scored by an LLM judge, the agent results average three runs with large spreads, and some baselines are values reported by their authors.

sections.title: Ethics and Broader Impact Statement
sections.content: MIRIX-2.0 lets assistants and task agents carry what users told them, and what the agents learned, from one session to the next. Every graph fact cites the records it was extracted from, so an answer can be traced to stored evidence. It is intended for assistants that users knowingly choose to use and should not be used to build profiles of people without their consent. user-centric memory accumulates personal and possibly sensitive information. MIRIX-2.0 keeps sensitive verbatim values in Knowledge Vault that the hypergraph does not index, but this does not replace consent and access control. deployment should let users view, correct, and delete their memories, confine each memory to its user (Rezazadeh et al., 2025), and use model providers or local models that meet its privacy requirements, because stored content is sent to the model. Memory can also make mistakes persistent (Zhang et al., 2026a; Shang et al., 2026), and content injected into conversation can be stored and later retrieved as if it were trusted. wrong merge changes only the index, and procedural edit keeps citation only after its quote is checked, but in high-stakes settings learned skills and merged identities should still be reviewed by person and stored memories audited periodically (Ma et al., 2026b). All experiments use publicly released benchmarks under their licenses. We collected no new data and ran no study with human participants. MemoryCD is built from public Amazon product reviews, and we use it as released without attempting to identify the reviewers.

sections.content: This appendix collects the details of Section 2 that the main text summarizes or leaves out, in the order of its subsections. For each part it states the constants, schedules, scoring rules, and examples, explains why they are designed as they are, and names the step of Algorithm 1 they belong to. A.1 Memory types, routing, and writing The Meta Memory Manager is the first call of the write path (Algorithm 1, line 2). The router reads the and input and selects the memory types it updates. Each selected writer then reads the current store produces record that line 3 commits to the evidence plane before any graph work begins. Formally, each input xt is mapped to subset of six specialized writers, 1 Kt = Rθ(xt), = Wk(xt, m(k) 1 ), Kt, (A.1) and each writer owns the schema and update operations of one memory type. Both steps of (A.1) are language-model calls, which is why the router and the writers carry the mark in Algorithm 1. Table 5 lists the six types. The separation is functional. Only episodic and semantic memory are indexed by the hypergraph, because they hold the event and relational evidence that cross-memory traversal needs. The other types keep their direct, type-specific retrieval paths. Core memory holds the persistent state of the user and the agent, procedural memory holds the skills that Section 2.5 refines, resource memory holds documents and multimodal artifacts, and the knowledge vault holds sensitive verbatim values. Each of them is read through its own typed path rather than through the graph. In Algorithm 1, the test {episodic, semantic} is the only step of the write path that depends on whether record is graph-indexed. In Figure 2, both user turns are routed to the episodic and semantic writers. Source-faithful writing. Before record reaches the graph extractor, the writer prompts of our runs ask the episodic and semantic writers to keep complete lists, names, counts, titles, locations, and dates in the records details instead of replacing them with topical gist. Episodic writers store the time an event happened rather than the time it was mentioned, and they store planned event with its planned date. Write ordering. The write to the vector database commits before graph construction begins (line 3). Graph extraction is fail-soft indexing hook, so graph failure is logged but never rolls back stored memory. The evidence plane is thus the durable system of record rather than side effect of graph construction. A.2 Anchor admission, canonicalization, and frame extraction This part details lines 5 to 9 of Algorithm 1, which turn committed episodic or semantic record into the anchors and frames of Section 2.3. Anchor keys and admission. The key κ(n) of an anchor name normalizes case, punctuation, articles and other function words, word order, and conservative singular and plural variants while keeping numbers. In the code it lowercases the name, replaces punctuation with spaces, drops fixed list of eleven articles and function words, singularizes tokens of at least four letters, and sorts the remaining tokens, so that Mobile App and Mobile Apps share one key. The key is deliberately conservative. Numbers and dates are preserved, so 10 Gallons and 20 Gallons stay distinct, and only plural endings are normalized, so Training and Trains stay apart. single admission gate rejects generic filing terms, such as advice, details, information, plan, and tips, and dialogue-role pseudo-entities such as user and assistant, and it keeps at most 16 anchors for an episodic record and 18 for semantic one. The caps bound the anchor space of user, and they are sized for the arguments of an assertion rather than for bag of keywords, so that one frame with seven arguments does not exhaust them. The gate is the Admit call of Algorithm 1, and because it runs on the canonical key, one entry such as user also blocks User, Users, and the user. Registry-guided canonicalization. For every extracted entity, approximate nearest-neighbor search retrieves up to four existing anchors of the user whose cosine similarity is at least 0.72, and one language-model call per record makes conservative same-entity decision for all of its entities. The call is instructed not to merge different quantities, different days or months, different form or model codes, or related but distinct concepts. Canonicalization runs before the admission gate, which is the order Admit(Canon(Φ)) of Algorithm 1, so the gate judges canonical names rather than surface forms. The candidates come from the anchors the user already has, which is what keeps naming consistent as the graph grows and why we call the step registry-guided. Frames, literals, and repair. The extractor behind (5) is instructed to keep dates, prices, counts, durations, and measurements as literals on the frame rather than as anchors, so that values such as 7, $420, or three months stay attached to the assertion they qualify. frame is materialized only if its arguments resolve to at least two distinct anchors of the user, which is the test Af 2 of Algorithm 1. When deterministic audit finds that the extraction misses high-signal source details, such as quoted phrases, numbers, or concrete visual content, one bounded repair call may add frames that the source supports. The repair cannot remove anything the primary extraction produced. The audit compares the words of the rendered frames with the source text. It lists the quoted phrases and the numbers of the source that the frames do not cover, it treats source with visual content as uncovered when the frames cover less than 45 percent of its content words, and it sends at most twelve missing items to the repair call. missing date alone does not trigger repair, because session dates recur in many records and are already preserved by provenance. missing date is added to call that missing quote, number, or visual detail already requires. The planner (9) fixes two row budgets for every query, and Table 6 lists them by operator. The budgets grow with the operator, because counting and set construction need broader evidence than single-value lookup. single-value question needs the one row that holds the value, so its cited-row budget is the smallest, whereas count has to see many members of the set it counts. The evidence question inspects is therefore bounded by its operator and not by the length of the history. Anchor entry. Beyond the fifteen anchors that vector recall returns, relation query adds up to sixteen anchors that the question names exactly before the union is scored by (10). Person hubs receive larger penalty unless relation query names them explicitly. Only the exactly named anchors carry degree and predicate information, so the hub and predicate terms act on them alone. The two entry routes serve different questions. Vector recall finds the anchors whose names paraphrase the question, and exact lookup finds the anchors that relation question names, so that the relation lane can start from the named participants rather than from their nearest paraphrases. Two evidence lanes. The lanes follow three rules beyond those of Section 2.4. In the base-recall lane, same-chunk support and immediate temporal neighbors are recomputed from the provenance stored in the vector database instead of being duplicated as graph bookkeeping edges. In the relation-citation lane, predicate filtering runs inside Neo4j before the cap of 240 frames, and when the question names concrete object, only frames that contain it are kept. The base lane is the Rows(Aq) term and the relation lane the Adj(Aq, Pq) Single Temporal Intersection List-union Count BB 6 6 7 7 BR 4 6 7 9 12 23 term of Algorithm 1. Recomputing same-chunk and temporal neighbors from provenance keeps the graph free of edges that only restate what the evidence plane already records. Filtering by predicate inside the database before the cap means that an explicitly named hub with hundreds of incident frames does not trigger full traversal, and the frames that survive the cap are selected by deterministic order on the frame identifier, so which frames pass does not depend on the traversal order of the database. Fact scoring. Two details of (11) complete Section 2.4. When frame has no extracted event time, the state term sstate falls back at half weight to the time of the source record, so the frame can still compete on time. For intersection questions, hard shared-object group is preserved before these soft refinements, so recency cannot replace evidence that satisfies only one side of the intersection. The role term reads the typed roles of frame, and the state term reads the status literal that marks an event as planned or completed (Section 2.3), which is how planned events are penalized in count, list-union, and temporal questions. Citation-balanced fusion. Rows in each lane are reranked with shallow vector-rank prior and the lexical coverage of the query. Fusion runs separately for episodic and semantic rows within the row limit of request. Near-duplicate episodic paraphrases are collapsed only when they share calendar date, so the same wording on two different dates stays separate. Cited rows are filled first because graph fact without the row that supports it would leave the answer unverifiable, and the date condition on paraphrase collapse is the retrieval-side counterpart of the occurrence identity (7), which keeps undated repetitions apart at write time. A.4 Answer-time verification The Answer procedure of Algorithm 1 belongs to the evaluation harness rather than to the memory server, and the rule-based check of Section 2.4 never inspects reference answer. The check fires when it finds explicit uncertainty, count without number or one that disagrees with listed count, temporal answer without time, an answer number or month that is absent from the evidence ledger and the question, ledger evidence with an incompatible role, or planned event in count question. It also fires on every intersection question. The extra search uses query derived from Π(q), or the question itself for relation query. Most triggers mark way in which draft falls short of the evidence it was given or disagrees with it. number or month that appears in neither the ledger nor the question was not retrieved, count that disagrees with listed count contradicts the evidence, and planned event in count question would count something that has not happened. Intersection questions always trigger the check because they need evidence for both sides, and first retrieval that satisfies one side can look complete. The rewrite is line 19 of Algorithm 1, so the procedure adds at most one search and one model call to question. A.5 AutoDream schedule, candidates, and procedural refinement This part details the SemanticDream and ProceduralDream procedures of Algorithm 1 (lines 22 to 29) and expands Section 2.5. Invocation protocol. Semantic AutoDream is an explicit service call that never schedules itself. In our protocol, the ingestion driver invokes AutoDream after every five chunks and once after the final chunk. The chunk identifiers of each call resolve to the newly written semantic rows, which define the frontier of (12), and the eligible anchors backed by those rows are the sources of (13). An intermediate call therefore examines only the anchors whose semantic rows the batch just wrote, and the final call also considers the eligible anchors that no earlier call used as source. Candidate generation. The identity-stable types Tsafe of Section 2.5 are person, organization, location, object, and concept. Anchors of the types event, date, content, method, and other are excluded deliberately, because merging two of them can collapse distinct occurrences or temporal context even when their names are close in embedding space. Both endpoints of candidate pair must be backed by semantic rows and share the same eligible type, and the cosine threshold 0.86 of (13) is the index score 0.93 under the (1 + cos)/2 scale of Section A.2. Bounded schedule. An intermediate Dream verifies at most 80 unseen pairs from the current semantic delta. The final Dream considers the delta together with eligible anchors that have never served as Dream source, and it verifies at most 120 pairs. If that round merges anything, one repair round examines only the touched representatives and verifies at most 60 more pairs. Explicit negative decisions are cached by anchor type, so later cycles do not pay again to reconsider the same pair. The cache key hashes the case-folded pair in sorted order together with the type, so the order in which pair is encountered does not matter. Only explicit rejections are cached. pair that round did not reach within its cap is not recorded as rejected, so it becomes candidate again whenever one of its anchors is in later frontier. The intermediate rounds keep the graph consolidated while ingestion proceeds, and the final round sweeps up anchors that earlier rounds never used as source. In Algorithm 1, the cache is the set that line 22 subtracts from the candidate pairs, and the per-round caps bound the number of Same calls the loop makes. Procedural refinement. Two rules of the procedural path complete Section 2.5. The distiller judges the outcome of each pending session from quotes in its transcript, and an outcome whose quotes do not occur in the transcript is downgraded to unclear rather than trusted. Besides creating, editing, or deleting skill, the curator can mark an experience as already covered, not worth skill, or deferred, so it can decline an experience without changing the store. The quote check on outcomes and the quote check on citations are the procedural counterpart of the provenance that the hypergraph keeps for facts. They keep the skill library traceable although both Distill and Curate in Algorithm 1 are language-model calls. A.6 Invariants, learned decisions, and complexity Hard invariants. Four properties hold regardless of model behavior. 1. Every returned graph fact exposes the identifiers of its source memories. 2. Undated episodic occurrences from different memory rows receive different frame identities. 3. Retrieval and Dream both run under explicit candidate and output caps. 4. failed graph write cannot destroy committed memory, and graph read that raises an error falls back to direct evidence retrieval. Together with Equation (12), the first and fourth invariants give the source fidelity required in Section 2.1, the third gives bounded access, and the second gives temporal identity. Learned and deterministic decisions. Language models route inputs, write typed memories, extract frames, repair missing source details, judge semantic identity, and distill and curate procedural experience. Together with answer generation, these are the calls marked in Algorithm 1. Deterministic code owns the safety-critical boundaries, namely admissible anchor names, candidate allowlists, frame identities, the representation of events and their status, provenance attachment, query operators, lane budgets, merge algebra, and mutation order. An LLM may propose that two anchors are identical, for instance, but it cannot name an anchor outside the retrieved candidate set or delete evidence directly. Complexity. Let be the number of admitted anchors in one memory, the number of frames extracted from it, KA the anchor-retrieval cap, and KF the adjacent-frame cap. Ignoring model inference and indexed database lookups, writing memory into the graph costs O(d + h). Post-retrieval ranking and fusion cost O(KA + KF + KM ), where KM is the operator-dependent cited-row budget, and the system never materializes an unbounded evidence set from the vector database. For Dream frontier of size u, nearest-neighbor generation costs O(u log Au) under the vector index, and LLM verification is capped at 80 pairs per intermediate cycle and 180 pairs across the two possible final rounds. The constants behind these symbols are the ones of this appendix. The admission gate bounds by 16 for an episodic record and 18 for semantic one (Section A.2), KA is the fifteen anchors kept after scoring, KF is the cap of 240 frames, and KM is BR , at most 12 (Section A.3). The 180 final pairs are the 120 of the final round plus the 60 of its repair round (Section A.5). A.7 Implementation and an example hypergraph Evidence rows are stored in vector database and the hypergraph in Neo4j. Figure 9 shows part of the hypergraph that MIRIX-2.0 builds for LoCoMo conversation conv-26, in which Caroline and Melanie talk from May to October 2023. The full graph has 792 anchors, 1,379 frames, and 3,303 role edges. The figure keeps the 32 anchors that appear in the most frames, leaving out generic duplicates such as Family and kids, together with the 448 frames that join at least two of them. The two speakers are the largest hubs, with 650 and 529 frames. Topics that one speaker raises gather on that speakers side, such as the pride parade and Becoming Nicole for Caroline and pottery and her family for Melanie. The 94 frames that join only the two speakers lie between the hubs and are drawn in gray, and 25 painting and art are reached from both sides. Each frame also keeps role labels, literals such as dates, and citations to its source records, which the figure leaves out. Through these frames one anchor gathers evidence across sessions. Self-Acceptance appears in 13 frames from 10 sessions, which link it to the LGBTQ support group, the pride parade, Becoming Nicole, and Carolines painting Embracing Identity. Figure 9 The 32 anchors with the most frames in the conv-26 hypergraph and the 448 frames that join them. Anchors are colored by type and sized by frame count, and frames take the color of their nearest topic. We built this graph with graph indexing and AutoDream enabled, using Claude Haiku 5.5 for extraction and Cohere Embed v4 for embeddings instead of the models described in Section 3.1.
